fable-5.1.text:
So I think there are a few ways to look at it. Let me try to describe how I saw it at the time, and how I see it now.

The deep learning conviction was always something like this: you have a big neural network, and the brain is a big neural network, and if the brain can do it, then a sufficiently large artificial neural network can do it too, provided you train it the right way. That belief existed before the scaling era. What was missing was a recipe. In the age of research, you needed an idea. You would try something, and maybe it worked, and maybe it didn't, and it was hard to know in advance.

The thing that happened with pre-training is that it turned a question that required ideas into a question that required resources. You take the objective, which is next token prediction, something very simple, almost embarrassingly simple. You take a lot of text. You take a big network. And you discover that as you make everything bigger, the model gets better in a very smooth, very predictable way. The scaling laws made it legible. You could show a chart to someone and say, if we spend ten times more, here is roughly what we get. That is an unusual property for a research field to have. Most of the time you cannot promise anything.

Now, why does such a simple objective produce something so capable? I think the answer is that text is not random. Text is produced by people, and those people had some understanding of the world when they wrote it. So if you want to predict the next word very well, not approximately, but really well, you are forced to learn something about the process that generated the text. You end up with a compressed version of what people know. The prediction is the surface, but what you are actually learning is underneath it.

So the breakthrough, in my view, wasn't one trick. It was the realization that this particular combination had no obvious ceiling in sight, and that you could just keep going. For a while, that was enough. You didn't have to be clever, you had to be committed. And it is only now, when the easy part of that is starting to run out, that we are going back into something more like the age of research again.

opus-5.5.text:
I think the way to understand it is that pre-training gave people a recipe. Before that, machine learning progress felt like research in the purest sense. You had ideas, you tried them, most didn't work, and you couldn't easily predict which one would pan out. It was hard to know where to put your resources.

Then pre-training came along, and the insight was almost embarrassingly simple. You take a big neural network, you take a lot of data, basically a large chunk of the text humans have written, and you train the network to predict what comes next. And it turns out that if you do this at larger and larger scale, with more compute, more data, and bigger models, the results get better in a remarkably predictable way. That's the key thing: the predictability.

There's also something deep about it intellectually. To predict the next word really well, you have to understand a lot. You have to understand the world that produced the text, the people who wrote it, their reasoning, their mistakes. So this one simple objective forces the model to pick up a huge amount of structure. It's not obvious in advance that it should work as well as it does, but it does.

I think it's also worth noticing what the word "scaling" did. It's a very powerful word, because it tells you what to do. It says: take this thing and make it bigger. For organizations, that was enormously attractive, because it turned a risky research bet into something much closer to an engineering and investment problem. If you put in this much compute and this much data, you get this much improvement. Compared to funding open-ended research, where you might spend a lot and get nothing, that's a very low-risk way to deploy resources. So everyone converged on it.

But that strength is also a limitation. Pre-training data is finite. At some point you've used it up, and then the question becomes: what do you scale next? Either you find a different recipe, or you find a way to use your compute more productively than just adding more of the same. So in some sense I think we're moving from an era where scaling was the answer back to an era where research matters a great deal again, just with much bigger computers than before.

r002.rationale: It describes pre-training as a recipe whose results improve predictably with more compute, data, and larger models.

fable-5.text:
You know, I think the way to understand it is that pre-training gave people something very rare in machine learning, which is a recipe. Before that, progress in AI required ideas. You had to be creative, you had to invent something, and inventions are unpredictable. But pre-training said: here is a simple objective — predict the next word — and here is a very large neural network, and here is a lot of data and a lot of compute. And if you put these together, you get something that works, and if you put in more, it works better. So suddenly you could convert resources into intelligence in a way that was legible. Companies could look at it and say, if we spend this much compute, we will get this much improvement. That de-risked everything, and that's why it took off.

But I think there's a deeper reason it works at all, which is less obvious. When you train a model to predict the next token well, you might think it's just learning surface statistics, correlations between words. But to predict the next token really well, you need to understand the process that produced that token. The text is a projection of the world — of the people, their thoughts, their situations. So good prediction forces the model to learn a compressed representation of the underlying reality. It's compression, really. And the surprising empirical discovery was that our large neural networks, trained with backpropagation, are actually capable of representing that — that the artificial neuron is not so different from the biological neuron in what it can achieve, if you have enough of them. People didn't believe that for a long time. The breakthrough was partly technical, but it was also partly just daring to believe that the simple thing, done at scale, would work.

r003.rationale: It says the predictable recipe made progress legible, let companies estimate improvement from compute spending, and “de-risked everything,” contrasting it with unpredictable invention.

opus-5.text:
The thing that was special about pre-training — and it took me a while to really appreciate how special — is that it was a *recipe*. For most of the history of machine learning, you had a situation where lots of smart people had lots of ideas, and all the ideas were beautiful in their own way, and there was no way to know which one was correct. You'd try something, you'd get a result slightly better or slightly worse than the last thing, and the signal was so weak that the field actually moved by taste. By fashion, almost.

Pre-training was different because it said: here is a thing you can do, and if you do more of it, it will be better. More compute, more data, bigger model — better. And the remarkable property, the thing I think people underrate, is that it required no ideas. You did not need to be clever. That is an extraordinarily unusual property for a research direction to have. And it meant the research could be de-risked, which is what unlocked the capital. You could go to someone and say, I want a very large amount of compute, and I can tell you in advance that the model will be better, and here is a straight line on a log plot that says so. That had never really been possible before.

I also think there's a deeper reason it works, which is that predicting the next token is secretly a very demanding task. To predict text from the internet really well, you have to model the process that produced it, and that process is people — with their beliefs, their moods, their errors. So the compression gives you a model of the world almost as a byproduct. Nobody asked for that. It falls out.

But recipes have ingredients. And the ingredient here is data, and there is only one internet. Compute keeps growing — the clusters keep growing — and data does not. So I've come to think of pre-training as an era rather than the answer.

sonnet-5.5.text:
I'd say there were two things, and they're related.

The first is the idea that the neural network is a very general, very powerful thing. If you make it big enough and train it on enough data with a simple objective, it learns more and more of the structure in that data. In the case of pre-training, the objective is to predict the next token. That sounds almost too simple, but to predict text well you have to model what produced the text, which is people, with their thoughts, feelings, and the world they live in. So the more accurately you predict, the more of that you capture. I think that's why it kept working.

The second is that it gave you a recipe. Before that, progress in machine learning felt like a search for the right idea, and every project carried a lot of research risk. You never knew whether the next thing would work. With pre-training, and especially once the scaling laws showed up, you could say that if you put in this much compute and this much data, you'd get a model this good. That's a very compelling thing, because a company can invest in it with confidence. It's low-risk compared to doing research, where you have to find something new and may find nothing.

That's also why it absorbed so many resources. The recipe was predictable, and for a while it just kept delivering. Data is finite, though, so at some point you have to ask what comes after it.

haiku-5.5.text:
I think it was less a single insight than a bet that kept paying off. For a long time the field leaned on clever architectures and hand-built structure. What kept striking me was that if you took a neural network and made it bigger, gave it more data and more compute, it kept improving in a fairly smooth and predictable way. That predictability is the remarkable part, because it means you can decide how much to invest before you've spent it.

I think the deeper reason has to do with what prediction demands. If you train a model to predict the next token across a huge amount of human-written text, you're asking it to model whatever produced that text: the facts, the reasoning, the intentions of the people writing. To predict well, the model has to build internal representations of a lot of the world. Compression is a useful way to think about it. Getting very good at predicting data is closely tied to understanding it.

But the bet needed several things to line up at once: an architecture general enough to absorb scale, optimization that still works at large sizes, and data rich enough to keep rewarding extra capacity. None of those alone would have been enough. I'm honestly not sure how far the curve continues. The question I find most interesting now is which capabilities will keep coming from this same process and which will need something else.

astra-6.text:
I think the key insight is that prediction can be a very powerful form of learning. You take a neural network and ask it to predict the next word. That sounds like a very limited task. But what does it actually take to do it really well?

If you’re reading a detective story, at some point you might need to figure out who committed the crime to predict what comes next. If you’re reading an argument, you need to understand the argument. So the task is simple to specify, but the things you need to learn to solve it can be very sophisticated.

And the other important part is that you get the training signal from the data itself. You don’t need someone to sit down and label every example. The text gives you both the question and the answer. That makes it possible to train on a very large amount of information.

But that alone doesn’t establish that scaling will work. You also need the empirical observation that, as you make the network bigger and train it on more data, it keeps getting better. Once you see that reliably, you have something very compelling: a simple training procedure where more computation can translate into learning more about the world.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key realization was that prediction can be a very powerful way of learning. It sounds like a narrow task: you’re just trying to predict the next word. But what does it take to predict the next word really well? You need to understand what the text is talking about. You need to understand the situation, what people know, what they want, what might happen next. All of those things help you predict.

So you have this very simple training objective, but the task underneath it is extremely rich. And you can get the training signal directly from the data. You don’t need someone to separately specify every concept that the model should learn.

Then the empirical question is: does a larger neural network actually use the additional capacity to learn those things? Does giving it more data and more computation keep helping? Once you see that it does, scaling becomes a very compelling approach. You have a direction in which you can make progress, and you can measure that progress.

That’s the important combination: a simple objective, an enormous amount of available supervision, and a learning system that keeps getting better when you give it more resources.

terra-5.6.text:
The key realization was that next-token prediction is an incredibly rich learning signal. The data supplies its own labels, so unlike supervised learning, you are not limited by how much annotation people can produce. If you make the model large enough and train it on enough diverse data, the most effective way to predict what comes next is to acquire a great deal of knowledge about the world, language, people, and eventually reasoning.

Transformers made that objective practical to scale. Then you had this unusually clean recipe: more compute, more data, bigger models, and a loss that kept improving in a fairly predictable way. That is what made pre-training so compelling—it converted progress in machine learning into something that could be pursued systematically at scale.

luna-5.6.text: I think the breakthrough was realizing that you didn’t need to keep inventing a new learning algorithm for every capability. You could take a very general objective—predict the next token—train on an enormous amount of data, and then simply make the model larger and give it more computation. What was surprising was how reliably performance kept improving with scale. The loss went down in a remarkably smooth way, and as the models became larger, they began to acquire capabilities that nobody had explicitly programmed into them. So scaling pre-training became compelling because it turned progress into something systematic: more data, more compute, and a larger model produced a more capable system, rather than a collection of brittle, task-specific improvements.
